mcqs.question: At each step of the two-pointer intersection scan, which interval should you advance past?
options: Whichever interval has the smaller start value
Always advance both pointers together, one step each
Whichever interval was added to the result most recently
Whichever of the two current intervals ends first — since it cannot overlap anything still ahead in the other list
mcqs.explanation: Once an interval's end falls behind the other list's current interval, every remaining candidate in the other list starts even later, so the ended interval has no unfinished overlaps left to check and can be retired. Start value alone doesn't determine this, and advancing both together can skip a valid overlap.

mcqs.question: Why does concatenating both interval lists, sorting the combination, and merging fail to solve Interval List Intersection correctly?
options: It loses track of which original list each interval came from, so it can no longer distinguish a cross-list overlap from within-list adjacency
It's correct but runs in exponential time
It fails only when both lists have exactly the same length
Sorting a concatenated list is not possible if the two lists have different lengths
mcqs.explanation: The problem is fundamentally about finding overlaps between two distinct lists, and merging discards exactly the provenance information needed to tell that apart from ordinary within-list structure. It isn't a runtime or length issue — it's a correctness issue from throwing away which list each interval belongs to.

mcqs.question: What guarantees it's safe to permanently discard an interval once it's the earlier-ending one in a comparison?
options: Both lists being sorted by start and internally non-overlapping, which means every later interval in that list starts even later, so it can't overlap anything the other list still has ahead
The fact that intervals never share exact boundary values
The assumption that both lists have the same number of intervals
The fact that the intersection result is always smaller than either input list
mcqs.explanation: Sortedness and internal non-overlap are exactly what let you conclude that the retired interval's own list has nothing left that could still overlap the other list's current position. List lengths, exact shared boundaries, and result size have no bearing on this guarantee.

mcqs.question: Merge Intervals and Interval List Intersection both sweep over sorted intervals. What's the actual difference in what each algorithm maintains?
options: Merge Intervals requires two pointers while Intersection only needs one
Merge Intervals tracks a single running union across one list; Intersection tracks pairwise overlap between two independently advancing lists, and needs no sort since both are already sorted
They maintain the same invariant, just applied to a different number of input lists
Intersection is only a special case of Merge Intervals run twice
mcqs.explanation: The invariants are genuinely different: one collapses a single list into its disjoint union with one running "current merge," the other compares two separately-sorted lists and emits every pairwise overlap, needing two pointers and no sort at all. It's the reverse of pointer counts stated in option A, and it isn't reducible to running Merge Intervals twice.

mcqs.question: Interval List Intersection is O(n + m) rather than O(n log n + m log m). What makes the sort unnecessary here?
options: Because intersection results are always smaller than either input, sorting doesn't affect the final answer
Because the two-pointer scan implicitly sorts both lists as a side effect
Because the problem gives both lists as already sorted and internally non-overlapping, so re-sorting would be wasted work on a precondition that's already satisfied
Because O(n + m) and O(n log n + m log m) are equivalent for interval problems specifically
mcqs.explanation: The precondition that both lists arrive sorted is exactly what the algorithm exploits — spending time re-sorting data that's already sorted would be the same wasted-work mistake covered in Insert Interval. The two complexities are not equivalent in general, and the scan doesn't perform any sorting itself.
